rv.q: On the surface, 'The Scottsboro Boys' is a hard sell in a Times Square dominated by escapist fluff. The show was slightly tweaked after its off-Broadway run in the spring -- to give the characters more back story and motivation -- but it hasn't been compromised, and remains grimly thought-provoking.

Of the handful of Kander & Ebb collaborations at various stages of completion when lyricist Fred Ebb died in 2004, this provocative piece appears the likeliest to earn a place among the veteran songwriting team's signature shows.
Not since Sondheim's Assassins has an apparent mismatch between form and content been exploited with such savage pertinence.

The talent onstage is so lavish it overwhelms our comfortable pieties with pure showmanship, conjuring your applause in waves, then quietly placing an asterisk after each bravura number: Did I just clap for … a shuck-and-jive?
In an age when institutional racism endures in more veiled forms, this bold musical keeps you tapping your feet while it socks you with an emotional punch to the gut.
The show's creators have fashioned a work that is at once devastatingly sad and buoyantly entertaining.
Perhaps with a more nuanced book and flexible frame, Scottsboro would have more punch.
Ultimately, alas, the songs aren't tough or surprising enough to take us beyond contrasts of tragedy and minstrelsy.

But the music in “The Scottsboro Boys,” with its ragtime-rich score by the estimable team of John Kander and Fred Ebb (who died in 2004), will be softer on the ears of those who prefer the shapely melodies of traditional musical theater to the shriek of today’s electric guitars.
I can't imagine a nastier-tasting recipe.
This is the best new musical of the year.
It’s still smashing, and it’s still shocking.
Susan Stroman's spare and seamlessly staged production, in which metal chairs are manipulated to represent different locations, is inventive and athletic.
'The Scottsboro Boys' sets a high bar for Broadway musicals this season.
Kander and Ebb's score is exceptional. If not their best, a couple of the songs ranks among my all-time favorites.
The hysterical criticism it’s occasioned is evidence of its success.
And while the result is thoughtful, vibrant entertainment, the earnestness and irreverence can seem self-conscious.
But for most of the evening, the adventurous show doesn't fit its parts together very well.
The Scottsboro Boys is an antic shindig with a dark heart…unique and powerful- an eruption of entertainment.

cn.t: Critics hail this daring Kander and Ebb musical as provocative and brilliant, praising its audacious use of minstrel show conventions to expose racism. Some find the jarring mix of tragedy and entertainment challenging, but most laud its powerful impact.

vs.sum: The Lyceum Theatre offers good sightlines and a charming Beaux Arts ambiance, but suffers from cramped seating and small restrooms. Ideal for intimate dramas, but patrons should be prepared for less comfort during their visit.

acc.note: 4 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No elevator. Infrared devices available.
